interviewQuestions.question: Why can one blocking syscall stall all threads in a many-to-one model?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because in many-to-one, every user-level thread you create is invisible to the kernel — the kernel only ever sees a single kernel-schedulable entity representing the whole process, no matter how many threads your userspace library thinks it's managing. All the scheduling among those user-level threads happens entirely in userspace, without the kernel's involvement at all.

So when one of those user-level threads makes a blocking system call — a disk read, a network recv — the call goes to the kernel, and the kernel blocks the *one thing it can see*: that single underlying kernel thread. It has no idea there were four other user-level threads ready to run inside that same process, because they were never kernel-visible entities it could independently schedule. The whole process freezes even though most of its logical threads had useful work to do.

I'd tie this to why it died out as a default: on a single-core machine in the 90s, this was a bearable trade for cheap thread switching. Once multi-core became standard, many-to-one also couldn't use more than one core (again, the kernel sees only one schedulable thing), which was the final nail — that's why Linux and Windows both moved to one-to-one.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the failure mechanically — kernel visibility, not just "it's a known limitation" — since that's what lets you reason about newer models like Go's goroutines correctly.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Many-to-one blocking problem

interviewQuestions.question: How do Go's goroutines get away with being far cheaper than OS threads while avoiding the classic many-to-one blocking bug?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Goroutines are user-level threads, but Go's runtime doesn't use plain many-to-one — it uses many-to-many. A pool of real OS threads (sized by `GOMAXPROCS`, typically matching CPU cores) sits underneath potentially hundreds of thousands of goroutines, and the runtime's own scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto that pool.

The part that actually solves the blocking problem: when a goroutine is about to make a blocking call, the Go runtime intercepts it (for network I/O, this typically routes through a non-blocking, epoll/kqueue-based network poller rather than a real blocking syscall; for calls the runtime can't avoid blocking on, it detaches the OS thread and hands off to a fresh or idle one). Either way, the OS thread that goroutine was riding isn't stuck — it goes on to run other goroutines, so one goroutine waiting on I/O doesn't freeze the others.

The cost side of the trade: goroutines start with a tiny, growable stack (a few KB, versus a few MB reserved for a typical OS thread), so spawning hundreds of thousands of them is cheap in a way that would be impractical with one-to-one OS threads.

**Testing:** whether you can explain *why* goroutines are cheap and safe rather than just knowing the marketing claim "goroutines are lightweight."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How goroutines solve the many-to-one problem

interviewQuestions.question: You're debugging a multi-threaded C program on Linux where all threads mysteriously stall at once whenever a single thread does a slow file read. What threading model would explain this, and how would you confirm it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The symptom — one blocking call freezing every thread — is the textbook signature of a many-to-one threading model, where the kernel only ever sees a single schedulable entity for the whole process. On modern Linux this shouldn't happen with the standard pthreads implementation (NPTL), which is one-to-one, so I'd suspect either a very old/custom threading library, a green-thread runtime that isn't handling this particular blocking call specially, or a userland coroutine library that's making a genuinely blocking syscall instead of a non-blocking one it forgot to intercept.

To confirm, I'd check `ps -eLf` or `top -H` for the process — one-to-one kernel threads show up as separate visible LWPs (light-weight processes) in these tools; if I only ever see one kernel-visible entity no matter how many logical threads the app claims to run, that's many-to-one. I'd also strace the process during the stall: if the blocking read shows up as a real blocking syscall on the only visible thread, and nothing else executes until it returns, that confirms it.

The fix, if it is many-to-one somewhere in the stack, is either switching to the OS's native one-to-one threads or, if using a green-thread/coroutine runtime, finding and fixing the specific call that isn't going through the runtime's non-blocking interception path.

**Testing:** whether you can turn the theoretical threading-model concept into an actual debugging procedure with real tools (`ps -eLf`, `strace`), not just recite the definition.
